title: MBIST in a chip
summary: The previous training wrote March tests on paper. This one builds the **hardware** that runs them inside the chip: controllers, collars around the memories, and the connection to the test access port. This topic gives the big picture.
objectives: Name the parts of a memory BIST system and what each does.
Follow one MBIST run from start to pass/fail.
Compare the main design choices: dedicated or shared controllers, serial or parallel testing.

blocks.md: A large chip has hundreds or thousands of memories. Each one needs a March test at full speed, and the results must reach the tester. Memory BIST solves this with a few kinds of blocks:

blocks.caption: Memory BIST in a system on chip

spots.title: Test access (TAP / IJTAG)
spots.md: The tester — or software inside the chip — starts the tests and reads the results through the **JTAG test access port** and an on-chip network of test registers (**IJTAG**). This is the subject of the next training.

spots.title: MBIST controller
spots.md: Runs the March algorithm: generates addresses, data and read/write commands, and collects pass/fail. One controller usually serves **several memories**.

spots.title: Collar (wrapper)
spots.md: A thin layer of logic around each memory: muxes that switch the memory between **functional** and **test** use, and often the comparator.

spots.title: Different memory types
spots.md: SRAMs, register files and ROMs are all tested by MBIST — with different algorithms. A ROM is only read, and its data is compacted into a signature.

spots.title: Functional logic
spots.md: In normal operation the memories belong to the CPU, buses and accelerators. During MBIST the collar disconnects them.

blocks.caption: The parts of a memory BIST system

blocks.title: You have met all of this before
blocks.md: The controller is the *BIST controller* of *BIST Foundations* (IDLE → RUN → DONE). The address and data generators are the hardware form of ⇑ / ⇓ and of the data backgrounds from *March Tests*. Only the comparator replaces the MISR: memory read data is **predictable**, so it is compared directly.

subsections.title: One test run, end to end

blocks.md:
1. **Configure** — through TAP/IJTAG the tester selects the controller, the memories, the algorithm and the options (backgrounds, diagnosis on/off).
2. **Start** — the controller switches the collars to test mode.
3. **Run** — at the memory's own clock speed, the controller executes the March test on one or several memories.
4. **Compare** — every read is compared with the expected data; a mismatch sets a **fail flag**.
5. **Done** — the controller raises *done*, switches the collars back to functional mode.
6. **Read out** — the tester reads *done* and *pass/fail* (and diagnosis data if any) through TAP/IJTAG.

steps.title: Configure
steps.md: Through the slow **JTAG clock** the tester selects controller, memories, algorithm and options.

steps.title: Start
steps.md: A single *start* signal crosses into the chip's fast clock domain.

steps.title: Run
steps.md: The March test runs at the **memory clock** — hundreds of operations for every JTAG clock.

steps.title: Compare
steps.md: Every read is checked as it happens; nothing has to wait for the tester.

steps.title: Done
steps.md: *done* and *pass* cross back to the JTAG side.

steps.title: Read out
steps.md: The tester shifts the result out through JTAG.

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the steps of an MBIST run in order.
items: Start: collars switch to test mode
Run the March test at speed
Compare read data, set fail flags
Done: collars back to functional mode

blocks.title: Slow outside, fast inside
blocks.md: The tester talks to the chip through a **slow** JTAG clock (a few to tens of MHz). The test itself runs at the **functional** memory clock (hundreds of MHz or more). Only the start and the results cross between the two.

blocks.caption: Dedicated controllers test everything in parallel; a shared controller saves area

tabs.label: Dedicated or shared
tabs.md: **One controller per memory** is simple and fast — every memory runs in parallel — but costs area for every memory. **One controller for many memories** saves area; the memories share the address and data generators. Real chips share, grouping memories that are physically close and use the same clock.

tabs.label: Serial or parallel
tabs.md: A shared controller can test its memories **one after another** (serial — low power, long time) or **all at once** (parallel — short time, high power). Memories of different sizes and widths need care: the controller must know when each one is finished.

tabs.label: Hard-wired or programmable
tabs.md: A **hard-wired** controller runs one or a few fixed algorithms. A **programmable** one loads the algorithm through IJTAG, so a stronger test can be used after the chip is made. Topic 4 compares both.

questions.text: What is the main job of the **collar** around a memory?
options: Switching the memory between functional use and test use, and often comparing read data
Talking to the tester through JTAG
Storing the golden signature of the CPU

questions.text: Why does memory BIST compare read data directly instead of compacting it in a MISR, as logic BIST does?
options: The expected memory data is known at every read, so it can be compared directly.
MISRs cannot be built for memories.
Direct compare needs a slower clock.

questions.text: Put the steps of an MBIST run in order.
Which clock runs the March test itself?
options: No clock — the test is asynchronous

questions.text: What is true about sharing one controller among several memories? Select **all** correct answers.
options: It saves area compared with one controller per memory.
The memories can be tested serially or in parallel.
Memories sharing a controller are usually physically close and on the same clock.
Shared memories cannot be tested at speed.

questions.text: The tester starts MBIST and reads its results through the test access port (JTAG / IJTAG).
